channel.title: Designer on Layer5 Documentation
channel.description: Recent content in Designer on Layer5 Documentation

item.title: Collaborative Editing
item.description: In this tutorial, you and a teammate work on the same design at the same time. You save a design, share it, watch your teammate join as a live collaborator, edit together, and run a short review in a comment thread. Along the way you learn the four separate mechanisms behind collaboration in Kanvas: the live session, access, comments, and saving. Each one explains a different part of what you see.

item.title: Add and Configure Components
item.description:
A component is one piece of infrastructure in a design, and its configuration is what Kanvas applies when you deploy. This guide covers placing components on the canvas, editing their configuration, and moving them around by duplicating, copying, and pasting.

You need a design open in Designer mode. Designer is the only mode that allows authoring.

Add a component 🔗

Kanvas offers several ways to place a component. All of them produce the same result: a component in the design, with its configurator open beside it.

item.title: Build Designs
item.description:
These guides cover the tasks you perform while authoring a design in Designer mode. Each one accomplishes a single task and assumes you know what a design, a component, and a relationship are. If you do not, read Designs and Components and Relationships first.

Authoring happens only in Designer mode. Operator mode shows the recorded state of your clusters and blocks adding, editing, duplicating, and deleting components.

Goal Guide
Add components, edit their configuration, lock, duplicate, copy, and paste them Add and Configure Components
Connect components and remove connections Create Relationships
Draw, label, and annotate a design with shapes, text, and lines Whiteboard on the Canvas
Keep frequently used models one step away in the dock Pin Models to the Dock
Group components by shared labels Work with Tags

For how Kanvas decides which relationships exist and keeps their configuration in sync, read Policy Evaluation.

item.title: Create Your First Design
item.description:
In this tutorial you build a small web application design in Kanvas Designer: a Deployment that runs the application, a ConfigMap that holds its settings, and a Service that exposes it. You start from an empty canvas, connect the components, and save the result. The saved design is the starting point for Deploy and Observe Your First Design.

Along the way you learn what a design is made of, how relationships express the way components depend on each other, and when and how Kanvas saves your work.

item.title: Designs and Components
item.description: A design is the unit of work in Kanvas. It is a declarative description of infrastructure that you author on a canvas, save as a versioned document, share with others, and deploy to your clusters. Components are the building blocks of a design: some represent real infrastructure that Kanvas deploys, and others are annotations that only explain the design. Knowing which is which, and how a design behaves when you save, share, and deploy it, tells you exactly what Kanvas will do with your work.

item.title: Getting Started
item.description:
Kanvas turns cloud native infrastructure into a design you can see, check, and deploy. This section takes you from an empty canvas to resources running in a Kubernetes cluster. Along the way you learn the four ideas that every other Kanvas page builds on, and which parts of Kanvas need a Meshery deployment of your own.

What you will learn 🔗

  • How a design is built from components, relationships, and configuration, and how Kanvas saves it.
  • How Kanvas checks a design before it touches a cluster.
  • How a design becomes running resources, and how Kanvas tracks them afterward.
  • Which capabilities work on hosted Kanvas and which need a Meshery you run.

The model in four steps 🔗

  1. Design. In Designer mode you describe infrastructure as a design: components (such as a Kubernetes Deployment or Service), the relationships between them, and their configuration.
  2. Validate. Kanvas checks the design against each component’s schema and attaches every error to the component and field that caused it; a dry run then checks the design against a real cluster without changing it.
  3. Deploy. Kanvas applies the design to the Kubernetes clusters you select and labels every resource it creates with the design’s identity.
  4. Operate. In Operator mode you see the recorded state of your clusters and can filter it to the resources that belong to one design.

Where do you want to work? 🔗

Kanvas runs in two places. Both use the same Designer, but only a Meshery you run can reach your clusters.

item.title: Import and Merge Designs
item.description:
Import turns an existing configuration into an editable design. Kanvas identifies the format from the file content, converts it to a Meshery design, and saves it as a new design in your account. The original file is not kept for download, so exporting later produces a new file from the current design.

Import works in Designer mode. The import action is hidden in Operator mode.

Choose how to import 🔗

Method Accepts Result
Import dialog, File Upload One local file New design, or merge into the open design
Import dialog, URL Import One direct http or https URL to a single file New design, or merge into the open design
Drag or paste onto the canvas One or more files One new design per file, or a merge prompt if the canvas is not empty
Catalog clone or open A published design Copy of the design, see Clone a Design
GitHub integration in Layer5 Cloud Files and folders in a connected repository One private design per valid file

The URL must point at a file, not a repository, a chart repository, or a directory. Folders cannot be imported directly: compress a Kustomize project or Helm chart into a single archive first.

item.title: Share a Design
item.description:
Sharing opens a private design to the people you name. Each grant is for one person, and it has no access level: a person who can open the shared design can also edit it and comment on it. You can also change a design’s visibility to make it open to everyone, and you can copy a link that points people to it.

This guide covers the task. For the reasoning behind the access model, read Collaboration Model. For a worked example with two people, follow Collaborative Editing.

item.title: Validate a Design
item.description:
Validation checks the configuration of each component in a design against the schema of that component’s definition. It runs in your browser, needs no cluster, and changes nothing. Run it while you build to catch missing or malformed fields before a dry run or a deployment spends time on them.

Before you start 🔗

  • Environment. Validation runs in a Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not run it and shows a self-hosted-feature prompt instead.
  • A non-empty design. The Actions menu is disabled while the design has no components. An unsaved design validates; Kanvas validates the design as it is on the canvas.
  • Permission. On mobile, the Validate Design permission gates the action. See Permissions by Role.

What validation checks 🔗

Checked Not checked
Each component’s configuration against the JSON schema of its registered definition, with all errors collected per component Relationships between components
Required fields, types, and formats, including 32-bit and 64-bit integers and integer-or-string values Dependencies, namespaces, and cross-references
Anything in the target cluster

Annotation components (text, shapes, and other visual elements) carry no infrastructure and are skipped. They are counted separately in the summary.

item.title: Create Relationships
item.description:
Relationships record how components connect, and Kanvas keeps related configuration in sync once they exist. You create some relationships by hand and Kanvas creates others when it evaluates the design. This guide shows which is which, how to create each kind, and how to remove or hide them.

Relationships work only in Designer mode. For what each kind means, read Relationships.

Kind You create it by You remove it by
Edge (network, mount, reference, and other edge subtypes) Picking an edge from a component’s handle and dragging to a target Selecting the edge and choosing Delete
Hierarchical, inventory Dropping a component onto a compatible parent Dragging it out, or choosing Move Out of Parent
Hierarchical, wallet Dropping a component onto a compatible host Deleting the component, or choosing Move Out of Parent
Hierarchical, alias Kanvas creates it during evaluation Deleting the alias component
TagSets (shared labels) Giving components matching labels Changing the labels so they stop matching
Annotation edge Drawing with the Pen tool Selecting the edge and choosing Delete

Create an edge relationship 🔗

Edge relationships connect components that exchange traffic or depend on one another, such as a Service and a Deployment.

item.title: Share a Design Across Organizations
item.description: In this tutorial, an Organization Admin at one company asks an engineer at another company to review a private design. By the end, you will have given someone outside your organization access to one design, held a review in a comment thread, and removed that access. Along the way, you will learn what a grant gives someone, where Kanvas checks permissions, and why the review itself has to happen in comments.

item.title: Deploy and Observe Your First Design
item.description:
In this tutorial you take the design you saved in Create Your First Design to a live Kubernetes cluster. You validate it, dry-run it against the cluster, deploy it, and then switch to Operator mode to see the running resources that belong to the design. You finish by undeploying it.

Along the way you learn the difference between checking a design against its schemas and checking it against a cluster, how Kanvas chooses where to deploy, and how Kanvas keeps track of the resources a design creates.

item.title: Dry-run a Design
item.description:
A dry run submits every component in the design to the Kubernetes API server of each target cluster as a server-side dry-run request. The API server validates the object exactly as it would on a real apply, including schema, field values, and admission, and then discards it. Nothing is created, updated, or persisted, so you can repeat a dry run as often as you like.

Before you start 🔗

  • A connected cluster. Meshery must hold at least one connected Kubernetes context. With none, the request fails with error meshery-server-1096, Kubernetes cluster is unavailable.
  • A non-empty design. The Actions menu is disabled for an empty design.
  • Permission. Dry run is gated by the Validate Design permission. See Permissions by Role.
  • A Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not run dry runs.

Meshery Server performs the dry run with the kubeconfig it holds. Meshery Operator, MeshSync, and the broker are not required.

item.title: Manage Designs
item.description:
A design is a single record in Layer5 Cloud. It has one owner, lives in one workspace, and carries a visibility (private, public, or published) and a version. These guides cover each way a design enters, changes state, and leaves that record.

Two defaults shape everything below. A design saved for the first time is public, whatever visibility the client requests. Every save of an existing design raises its patch version by one (0.0.1, 0.0.2, and so on).

item.title: Relationships
item.description: A relationship records how two components connect: one runs inside the other, one sends traffic to the other, one mounts the other’s storage, or both carry the same label. Relationships do more than draw lines. Each relationship definition names the configuration fields on both sides that must agree, so Kanvas can write values from one component into the other and keep the design consistent as you edit. The definitions come from the Meshery registry, not from Kanvas, so the set of relationships available to you depends on the models you use.

item.title: Review a Design with Comments
item.description:
A comment is a note on the canvas that holds a threaded conversation. Use comments to give feedback, record the reason behind a configuration choice, or ask a teammate a question next to the component it concerns. A comment is part of the design: it saves with the design, appears live to everyone who has the design open, and travels with clones and exports.

For how comments fit with live editing and access, read Collaboration Model.

item.title: Save Designs
item.description:
Kanvas saves a design for you. There is no Save button and no Save shortcut. Every change that alters the design, such as adding, moving, configuring, or deleting a component, renaming, editing a relationship, or merging, queues a save. The request is sent 3 seconds after your last change. Changes made while a save is in flight queue a new save when it finishes.

Saving needs a signed-in user or a guest session on kanvas.new, and an organization. It does not check a permission key.

item.title: Canvas Objects
item.description:
Everything on a Designer canvas is an object, and every object answers to the same small set of actions: add, select, copy, duplicate, lock, restyle, resize and delete. This page lists each object kind, each action, every style option and the limits that apply. Edges - the lines that connect objects - have their own section at the end.

Designer mode only. In Operator mode you cannot add, edit, duplicate, delete or rename objects, and live nodes discovered from a cluster are read-only in every mode. See Designer for how the two modes differ.

item.title: Clone a Design
item.description:
Cloning copies a design into your own workspace so you can change it freely. The clone is an independent record: later changes to the source never reach it, and edits to the clone never reach the source.

What you can clone 🔗

The server clones only designs whose visibility is public or published. A request for any other design fails with 403 “unauthorized to clone design”. That includes your own private designs. To copy one of those, open it and use Save as. See Save Designs. A missing source design returns 500 “could not find design”.

item.title: Deploy a Design
item.description:
Deploying applies the components in a design to the Kubernetes clusters in the environments you choose. Meshery Server does the work with the kubeconfig it holds: it creates each object, or updates it in place when it already exists. Deploying the same design again is safe and idempotent.

Before you start 🔗

  • A Meshery you run, with a connected cluster. The hosted kanvas.new site does not deploy; it shows a self-hosted-feature prompt. Meshery needs at least one connected Kubernetes context that belongs to an environment in your organization.
  • A non-empty design. The Actions menu is disabled for an empty design. An unsaved design deploys as it stands on the canvas.
  • Permission. The Deploy Design permission gates the action. See Permissions by Role. Selecting environments from the empty state also needs the Create Environment and Edit Environment permissions.
  • A provider session. Without a signed-in session the request fails before any event is raised.

Deploying does not need Meshery Operator, MeshSync, or the broker. Those make the result visible in Operator mode.

item.title: Policy Evaluation
item.description: Evaluation is how a design stays consistent. After you change a design, Kanvas runs it through the policy engine, which applies the registry’s relationship definitions: it identifies relationships, writes configuration across related components, and drops relationships that no longer hold. The engine returns the whole evaluated design, and Kanvas applies it back to the canvas. This is why a value you did not touch can change a moment after you edit a related component.

item.title: Validate and Deploy
item.description:
Four actions take a design from the canvas to running infrastructure and back. Run them in this order. Each one is stricter than the last and costs a little more.

Action Checks or changes Needs a cluster Changes the cluster
Validate Each component’s configuration against its schema, in your browser No No
Dry run The design against the Kubernetes API of each target cluster Yes No
Deploy Creates or updates every component’s object on the target clusters Yes Yes
Undeploy Deletes every component’s object from the target clusters Yes Yes

The deploy and undeploy flows are five-step wizards that run validation and a dry run for you, so you do not need to run them separately first.

item.title: Whiteboard on the Canvas
item.description:
Whiteboarding in Kanvas (3:41) follows one late-night incident from page to postmortem on a single live design. Its page has chapters and a transcript.

Whiteboarding lets you diagram freely on the same canvas as your infrastructure. You draw shapes, text, freehand strokes, and lines to explain intent, and they sit beside real components in one design. It is on by default and available on every plan.

item.title: Collaborate and Review
item.description:
A design is one record with one owner. These guides cover how other people reach it and how you discuss it with them. Access is per person and has no access level: everyone who can open a design can edit it. Comments are part of the design, and they work in Designer mode.

Goal Guide
Give specific people access, change visibility, copy a link, or revoke access Share a Design
Leave threaded comments, mention people, resolve threads, and control email Review a Design with Comments

Live co-editing needs no setup. When two people have the same saved design open, they see each other’s cursors, selections, and edits. Collaboration Model explains how live editing, access, and comments fit together. To try all three with a teammate, follow the Collaborative Editing tutorial.

item.title: Concepts
item.description:
Kanvas rests on one idea: a design is a declarative description of infrastructure. It records which components exist, how they relate to each other, how each one is configured, and any annotations that explain the intent. A design describes the state you want; it is not a script of steps to run.

Each part of Kanvas plays one role around that design:

  • Designer authors the design. You place components, connect them, and configure them on a shared canvas. Every save creates a new version, and collaborators can edit the same design at the same time.
  • Meshery validates and deploys the design. It checks the design against component schemas, dry-runs it against target clusters, and deploys or undeploys it on the Kubernetes contexts you choose.
  • Operator shows the running result. It displays live cluster state and links it back to the design: every resource Kanvas deploys carries the identity of its source design, so Operator can show exactly what one design produced.

Layer5 Cloud, as the remote provider, stores designs and their versions and governs who can see them. Every new design starts public; Designs and Components explains visibility in full.

item.title: Designer
item.description:
Designer mode is where you author a Kanvas design. You compose infrastructure from versioned components, configure each one against its schema, connect components with relationships, annotate the result, and validate or deploy it, all on one canvas that every collaborator edits at the same time. Designer works on intent: what you want to run. Operator works on live state: what is running.

A design is a shared document 🔗

Everything on the canvas is an entry in one design document: every component you configure, every relationship, and every annotation you draw. The canvas draws that document. Moving a node, applying a layout, or hiding a layer writes into the design. As a result:

item.title: Export Designs
item.description:
Export writes a design out of Kanvas so you can back it up, move it between Meshery deployments, hand it to Helm or kubectl, or put it on a web page. Every export is generated from the current state of the design. You cannot export an earlier version.

Export is a File menu action, disabled on an empty design. In Operator mode, Export instead downloads the open view as <view name>.json.

item.title: Pin Models to the Dock
item.description:
Pinning a model puts its icon in the dock at the bottom of the canvas, so you can reach its components without opening the full palette. Pins belong to your account. They are not stored per design or in the browser, so they follow you across designs, browsers, and devices.

Pinning works in Designer mode. In Operator mode the dock does not show pinned models.

Pin a model 🔗

Hover a model row in the component palette and use the pin icon. Its tooltip reads “Pin To Dock”. The shape palette offers the same pin on each shape category row.

item.title: Tool Modes
item.description:
The canvas has four tool modes. The mode decides what a mouse drag does: move an object, pan the view, draw freehand or draw a connecting line. Select is the default. This page lists how to enter and leave each mode, what every mouse gesture does in it, and the wheel and zoom controls that work in all of them.

Modes at a glance 🔗

Mode Purpose Enter Leave Drag on empty canvas Box selection
Select Select, move, configure and style objects. The default. V or Esc Choose another mode Draws a selection box On
Pan Move the view without touching objects. H, or hold Space V, Esc, or release Space Pans the view Off
Pencil Draw freehand annotations. Ctrl/Cmd + P, or the Pencil tool in the dock The same shortcut, V or Esc Draws a stroke Off
Pen Draw connecting lines and annotation edges. Ctrl/Cmd + E, or the Pen tool in the dock The same shortcut, V or Esc Places points and lines Off

The Pencil and Pen dock icons turn green while their mode is active. The mode shortcuts work in Designer mode. Select and Pan also work in Operator mode.

item.title: Undeploy a Design
item.description:
Undeploying deletes the Kubernetes objects that each component in a design describes, from every cluster in the environments you select. It does not touch the design itself. The design record, its versions, and its Operator view are unchanged.

Before you start 🔗

The prerequisites match Deploy a Design: a Meshery you run with a connected cluster, a non-empty design, and the Undeploy Design permission. The hosted kanvas.new site does not run undeploy. See Permissions by Role.

item.title: Canvas Actions
item.description:
Right-clicking an empty part of the canvas - anywhere no component sits - opens the Canvas Actions menu. Where the component context menu acts on one component, this menu acts on the canvas as a whole: undoing and redoing, pasting, selecting everything, capturing the canvas as an image, and reaching help.

The menu adapts to the mode you are in. Commenting and pasting, for example, are offered in Designer mode but not in Operator mode, where the canvas reflects discovered infrastructure rather than a design you are authoring.

item.title: Embed Designs
item.description:
An embedded design is an interactive picture of a design on your own page. Readers can pan and zoom it, but cannot edit it. It is a static export: Kanvas gives you a JavaScript module file and a snippet that loads it.

How an embed works 🔗

  • It is a snapshot. The file holds the canvas as it was at export time: node positions, element styles, and inline background images converted to data URLs where the fetch succeeded. Later edits to the design do not change an exported file. Re-export to refresh it.
  • It needs no Layer5 Cloud at view time. The page makes no request to Layer5 Cloud, so the embed works for private designs and keeps working if the design is deleted. Anyone who can read your page can read the embedded design data.
  • It is view only. Layout is fixed to the exported positions. Selection and box selection are disabled, zoom is limited to 0.5x to 6.6x, and there is no editing, component configuration, relationship evaluation, or live cluster data.
  • It loads one library. The page fetches the Cytoscape library (version 3.27.0) from a public CDN, so viewers need outbound access to it. A Meshery logo link, which opens meshery.io, is drawn at the bottom right of the canvas. No option removes it.
  • It has no parameters. Width, height, theme, background, and zoom are not options. The container’s CSS sets the size.
  • There is no iframe embed. Kanvas offers no embed URL for the app itself.

Embedding needs no permission key and no paid plan.

item.title: Work with Tags
item.description:
Tags are the key-value labels and annotations on a component. When components share matching labels, Kanvas groups them in a TagSet, a shaded region drawn around the matching components. Use tags to see which components belong together, such as the Service and Deployment of one application.

Add labels and annotations 🔗

Open a component’s configurator and go to its Labels tab. It holds two key-value maps:

item.title: Collaboration Model
item.description:
Collaboration in Kanvas, whether at kanvas.new or inside Meshery, rests on three separate layers that work together:

  • Live co-editing (presence) - people who have the same design open see each other’s cursors, selections, and edits as they happen.
  • Access - the design’s visibility and its grant list decide who can open and change the design.
  • Conversation (comments) - comment threads that live inside the design itself.

The three layers are independent. A live session forms between whoever has the design open at the same time. Access decides who can open the design in the first place. Comments are part of the design’s content, so they follow the design wherever it goes. Keeping these layers apart in your head explains most of what you see when a team works on one design.

item.title: Layout and Layers
item.description:
Two controls decide how a design reads on screen. Layout arranges the components - where they sit relative to one another. Layers decide which of them are drawn at all.

Both are recorded in the design rather than in your browser, so they travel with it: a layout writes the components’ positions, and the Layers panel writes their visibility into the design’s preferences. Anyone else opening the design sees the same arrangement and the same components hidden. What neither touches is configuration - a hidden component is still part of the design and is still deployed, and re-running a layout changes only where components sit.

item.title: Publish Designs
item.description:
Publishing makes a design discoverable in the Layer5 Cloud catalog, where anyone can view and clone it. Publishing is separate from visibility: making a design public does not publish it.

Visibility and publication states 🔗

State Who can read it How it gets there
Private Owner, provider administrators, and users with a share grant Cloning, unpublishing, or switching a public design to private
Public Anyone, including anonymous callers, who has the design’s id or link The default for every newly saved design
Published Everyone through the catalog An approved publish request, or a direct publish by an approver

The owner can toggle a design between private and public until it is published. A published design cannot be toggled. The toggle saves through the normal save path, so it raises the version and re-checks the components limit.

item.title: Component Badges
item.description:
A badge is a small marker Kanvas draws on the edge of a component to report something about it: errors waiting to be fixed, components held inside it, a link, or where it came from. Badges are status, not decoration. A count on a badge tells you there is something to read, and clicking it shows what.

Which badges appear depends on the mode. Designer mode draws badges that help you build a valid design. Operator mode draws badges about live resources.

item.title: Delete a Design
item.description:
Deleting a design removes the design record and its workspace mappings in one transaction. There is no trash and no restore. Export a copy first if you might need it. See Export Designs.

Who can delete 🔗

The server allows the design’s owner or a provider administrator. Organization administrators, workspace owners, and collaborators with a share grant cannot delete a design (403 “unauthorized for the operation”). Layer5 Cloud hides its Delete action for roles without the Delete a Design permission, but the server decides by ownership, not by the key. To remove a design from a workspace without deleting it, use the workspace’s remove action instead.

item.title: Render Modes
item.description:
Render mode sets how much detail Kanvas draws for a design. It works as a fidelity dial for your current session, not a property of the design. Switching modes never changes components, relationships, configuration, or layers, and the mode is not saved with the design. Every session starts in Full unless the URL sets a different mode. The switcher appears in the Options dialog and in the Designer toolbar.

What each mode trades away 🔗

Kanvas has four render modes. Each of the first three gives up something the mode above it draws.

item.title: How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud
item.description: Kanvas is not a standalone service. It is an extension that runs inside Meshery, relies on Meshery Server to reach your clusters, and relies on a remote provider, Layer5 Cloud, to store and share designs. Knowing which part does what explains why some features need a cluster connection, why others need an account, and why the hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new offers a subset of what a self-hosted Meshery deployment offers.

item.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
item.description:
Kanvas binds every shortcut to both modifier keys. On Windows and Linux use Ctrl. On macOS use Cmd. The tables write the modifier as Ctrl/Cmd.

Kanvas ignores shortcuts while you type in a text field, so typing a label, a comment or a search never triggers one. Open the same list inside the app with Ctrl/Cmd + /.

Modes and navigation 🔗

Shortcut Action Designer Operator
V or Esc Switch to the Select tool. Esc also closes open menus and dialogs. Yes Yes
H Switch to the Pan tool. Yes Yes
Space (hold) Pan while the key is down, then return to the Select tool. Yes Yes
Ctrl/Cmd + P Turn the Pencil tool on or off. Yes No
Ctrl/Cmd + E Turn the Pen tool on or off. Yes No
Ctrl/Cmd + + Zoom in. Yes Yes
Ctrl/Cmd + - Zoom out. Yes Yes
\ (backslash) Open the Layers panel. Yes Yes
Ctrl/Cmd + / Open the shortcut reference in the help drawer. Yes Yes
Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + / Open the Help Center. Yes Yes

The tools are described in Tool Modes.

item.title: Kubernetes Request Flow
item.description: A request to an application in Kubernetes passes through several objects before it reaches a process in a container, and none of those objects is wired to the next by a fixed address. Each layer finds the next one by name or by label at the moment the request arrives. Knowing that path, and what each layer is responsible for, turns “why am I not getting a response?” into a short list of places to look. This page walks the path from the client to the container, explains why labels and selectors are what hold it together, and shows how the same path appears in a Kanvas design.

item.title: Troubleshoot Kanvas
item.description:
Kanvas separates two kinds of failure. A design action that fails, such as a dry run or a deployment, produces an event with an error code and a remediation. A Kanvas that fails to load, or an Operator view with no data, produces an in-product message. This page covers both.

Ask for help from within Kanvas

The Get Help action opens the Help and Support form. It needs a remote provider and a signed-in identity. See Help and Support.

Kanvas does not load 🔗

If an unhandled error occurs, or the extension fails to load in the Meshery shell, Kanvas shows Uh-oh! Something went wrong.. (Uh-oh! Please pardon our mesh. in the shell) with the error text. The screen offers:

item.title: Supported Import and Export Formats
item.description:
This page lists exactly what Kanvas accepts and produces. For the steps, see Import and Merge Designs and Export Designs.

Import 🔗

Kanvas accepts the extensions .yml, .yaml, .json, .tar, .tar.gz, .tgz, .gz, and .zip. Detection is by content and takes the first match in the order below.

Order Format Extensions Detected when Notes
1 Meshery design .yml .yaml .json The schema version is a supported design version Lossless round trip of a design file export
1 Meshery design as OCI image .tar .tgz .tar.gz .zip The archive’s layers contain a design file Only the first design is taken. Other layer files are ignored. No design file means failure.
2 Kubernetes manifest .yml .yaml One or more valid Kubernetes documents Multi-document files work. Unknown kinds are kept as generic objects.
3 Helm chart .tgz .tar.gz .gz .tar .zip A valid packaged chart An uncompressed .tar is reported as needing gzip. No values overrides.
4 Docker Compose .yml .yaml Converts as a Compose file The result is Kubernetes components.
5 Kustomize .yml .yaml (kustomization), or an archive containing kustomization.yaml The project builds Archive must contain every referenced file.

If nothing matches, the import fails and lists why each format was rejected. The interface shows only the generic failure message.

item.title: URL Parameters
item.description:
Kanvas reads its starting state from the query string of its address. A link can open a specific design, open Operator on a view, choose how much detail the canvas draws, and restore a zoom and pan position. The links produced by the Share dialog and by Copy Link are built from these parameters.

Append parameters to the Kanvas route of the Meshery you are using. On the hosted app that route is https://kanvas.new/extension/meshmap; on the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery it is /extension/meshmap on that host.

item.title: Auto-pan on Drag
item.description:
Auto-pan on Drag scrolls the canvas for you while you drag a component toward the edge of the view. Without it, moving a component to a part of the design that is off screen takes a drag, a manual pan, and another drag. With it, one continuous drag carries the component there.

Auto-pan is off by default. You turn it on as a personal setting, and Kanvas still switches it off while a design is too large for the current render mode.

item.title: Performance Limits
item.description: Kanvas draws a design on a canvas and redraws it on every pan, zoom and edit. The cost grows with the number of components and relationships and with how much detail each one carries. Kanvas controls that cost in four ways: the render mode you choose, gates that turn expensive features off past a design size or below a zoom level, Adaptive mode, which changes the render mode for you, and a small number of enforced limits.

item.title: Design Review Mechanics
item.description:
Use comments to offer feedback to team members, take detailed design notes, capture helpful tips for your team members, and include justification as to your infrastructure and application configuration decisions. Pay it forward to your future self by leaving historical record for reference later.

Lessons learned in this Peer Review module:

  • Collaboration is Key: Kanvas facilitates collaborative design through peer reviews. It emphasizes both asynchronous (commenting, notifications) and synchronous (real-time discussion) methods.
  • Clear Workflow: The script outlines a defined workflow for peer reviews, from requesting a review to providing feedback and reaching completion.
  • Specific Feedback: Kanvas allows users to provide feedback on specific components of a design, making the review process more targeted and effective.
  • Centralized Review: All feedback is stored within the Kanvas design, creating a centralized location for review and discussion.
  • Benefits of Peer Review: The script highlights the advantages of using Kanvas for peer review, such as improved collaboration, reduced errors, and faster design cycles.
  • Flexibility: The script allows for different methods of adding comments (drag and drop, toolbar icon, hotkey, right-click) to accommodate user preferences.
  • Notifications: Users receive notifications for review requests and comments, ensuring they stay updated.
  • Both Asynchronous and Synchronous Collaboration are Important: The demo covers both types of interaction.

Pinning Models to Dock
item.description:
Transcript:

Five has found that he frequently references the same set of models while designing. If you know that you’ll be using components from a model frequently, you can pin that model for easy retrieval of its components. To pin a model to the dock in Layer5 Kanvas, click the pin icon next to the model. The model will now be accessible in the dock for quick use.

item.title: Publishing Designs
item.description: Publishing a design lets you make your content visible to any anonymous visitor of https://cloud.layer5.io/catalog and any Layer5 Cloud user. Anyone with the link can view the design. You can publish the design into your Cloud Catalog.

item.title: Whiteboarding in Kanvas
item.description: At 2:47 AM, checkout latency is climbing and the architecture diagram cannot be trusted. Five, Mia, and Raj open the live checkout design in Kanvas and work the incident together on one canvas, using the whiteboarding tools that are on by default in every design. By morning, that same canvas is the incident record, the postmortem starting point, and the onboarding guide. (The incident and its telemetry are a demo scenario.)
